title: Did Xuanzang, the Real Tripitaka, Sneak Abroad? The Arrest Warrant Torn Up in 629
description:
In 629, the 3rd year of Zhenguan, Li Chang, a clerk of Guazhou prefecture, set an arrest warrant sent from Liangzhou before a young monk: "There is a monk styled Xuanzang who means to enter the western lands; the prefectures and counties where he is shall watch closely and seize him." The monk did not deny it.

This episode follows two biographies written by people of the Tang themselves. On his memorial in Chang'an, the Biography of the Tripitaka Master of the Great Ci'en Monastery (the Ci'en Biography) says "by edict, refused," while the Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks by his contemporary Daoxuan says the memorial was never passed on at all. Li Daliang, Governor of Liangzhou, ordered him back to Chang'an, and from then on he "hid by day and moved by night"; Li Chang tore up the warrant in front of him; the guide Shi Pantuo took him around the gate, 10 li upstream of Yumen Pass; at a beacon tower an arrow "nearly hit his knee"; his waterbag spilled, and he told himself "better to die going west than live by going back east"; Qu Wentai, King of Gaochang, "swore brotherhood" with him (Journey to the West gives that role to Emperor Taizong of Tang). On the way back, in a memorial from Khotan, he wrote in his own hand "defied statutes, went privately to India." In the 2nd month of Zhenguan 19 (645; months here follow the Chinese lunar calendar), he met Taizong at Luoyang Palace. Taizong asked "Why leave without telling me?"; he answered "I went privately, on my own: the crime of presumption"; Taizong said "no need for shame." Leaving the country without the court's permission: he admitted it himself, so that page is on record. Which year he set out: most Tang records say Zhenguan 3 (629), and only one memorial, collected in the Guang Hongming Ji, says Zhenguan 1 (627), so that one stays open.

Buddhist texts follow CBETA (Taisho base text, with collation notes); the official histories, the Zizhi Tongjian, the Tang Code with Commentary and Journey to the West follow Daizhige transcriptions. In "by edict, refused," the Taisho base text writes the character for "edict" in a variant form. The Tang Code is a later statute; the law in force when Xuanzang crossed the frontier has not survived. Sources are listed in the references below. This episode covers only the journey and where the texts come from, not matters of faith.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant as likenesses.

Information as of 2026-10-20 (rewritten on 2026-10-25 under new guidelines)

x001.text: Taizong's sworn brother Tripitaka left Chang'an with a travel pass, right?

x002.text: But 1,400 years ago, a warrant was chasing him.

x003.text: Guazhou, the Tang's far west. A clerk, the warrant tucked away, finds a young monk at a temple.

x004.text: It read: a monk named Xuanzang means to go west; all prefectures and counties, arrest him.

x005.text: The clerk asked just one thing: Master, isn't this you?

x007.text: That's not the worst: at a beacon tower past the pass, an arrow flew at him.

x008.text: Over a decade later, what did the emperor first ask him?

x009.text: This file follows the Tang's own biographies through his 17 years, from Chang'an to Luoyang.

x010.text: Did the Tang's best-known monk really sneak abroad?

x011.text: Back before Guazhou. In Chang'an, he had asked the court.

x012.text: With companions, he sent a memorial asking to go west for scriptures. The result?

x013.text: His disciple's Ci'en Biography says: by edict, refused.

x014.text: His companions all backed out; only he refused to give up. But did that memorial ever reach the emperor?

x015.text: But know this: another biography exists, by a man who met him.

x016.text: Monk Daoxuan's Continued Biographies is much gentler:

x017.text: The answer, per Daoxuan: it never got there. He sent it alone; no office passed it on.

x018.text: By this book, there was no edict of refusal. With no edict, was he free to go?

x019.text: So how did he go? Daoxuan: frost hit in Zhenguan 3 (629); the court let monks and folk seek food where crops grew.

x020.text: Using that chance, he went west to Liangzhou. The Ci'en Biography: he was 26 then.

x021.text: The catch: past Chang'an, the first hurdle wasn't desert, but people.

x022.text: And soon someone wanted him arrested.

x023.text: In Liangzhou, his first run-in: Governor Li Daliang.

x024.text: The biography: the young Tang barred people from leaving; Li Daliang, newly under strict orders, watched closely.

x025.text: Over a month there, he lectured in public.

x026.text: A Chang'an monk preaching over a month: who would hear of it?

x027.text: Someone told Li Daliang: a monk from Chang'an wants to go west.

x028.text: Li Daliang summoned him. The monk: to seek the Dharma in the west. Li Daliang ordered him back to Chang'an.

x030.text: No. A Liangzhou master secretly sent two disciples to sneak him west.

x031.text: Not daring to go openly, he hid by day and moved by night, reaching Guazhou.

x032.text: Guazhou's prefect Dugu Da was kind to him. He learned the way west had to pass Yumen Pass.

x033.text: Beyond it: five beacon towers, 100 li apart, no water or grass between.

x034.text: Yet the Liangzhou warrant followed him to Guazhou.

x035.text: Remember the clerk with the warrant at the start? Li Chang. That day, the monk told the truth.

x036.text: Li Chang: if you can really do it, I'll destroy the warrant.

x037.text: He tore up the warrant in front of the monk, adding: Master, go soon.

x038.text: If it were you, a wanted man before you, would you tear it up?

x039.text: Yumen Pass still lay ahead. His guide: a Central Asian who came to worship at the temple, Shi Pantuo.

x040.text: He asked for the precepts, then promised: I'll get you past the beacon towers ahead.

x041.text: He also brought an old man, who warned: the west road is deadly; no one has ever made it.

x042.text: Failing that, the old man swapped him his old red horse: 15 Yiwu round trips; it knew the way. Remember this horse.

x043.text: Near midnight, at the river, Yumen Pass far off.

x044.text: 10 li upstream, Shi Pantuo cut logs, laid grass and sand, drove the horses over.

x045.text: Later Tang law: no papers at a gate, 1 year's labor; skirting it, a grade worse.

x046.text: The law of his day is lost, but you can probably guess: no small thing. Was that debt ever collected?

x047.text: Soon after, Shi Pantuo suddenly drew a knife, neared the monk, turned back within 10 steps.

x048.text: The biography: the monk couldn't read him. Next day Shi Pantuo said: I won't go; big family; can't break the law.

x049.text: The monk swore: even if caught, I will never name you. There they parted.

x050.text: From here on, he led that old horse into the desert alone. Alone, could he make it out?

x051.text: First beacon tower: at night, he crept to water, crouched to drink.

x052.text: He'd just drawn his waterskin when something flew from the dark.

x053.text: Remember the arrow at the start? This one nearly hit his knee.

x054.text: A second came. He shouted: I'm a monk from the capital, don't shoot!

x055.text: The tower officer Wang Xiang learned who he was and urged: I'm from Dunhuang; I'll take you there.

x057.text: He answered: hold me or sentence me if you must; I won't take one step east.

x058.text: But Wang Xiang gave food and water, wept farewell, sent him to tower 4.

x059.text: Tower 4's Wang Bolong, Wang Xiang's kin, said skip tower 5: get water at Wild Horse Spring, 100 li off.

x060.text: Five beacon towers, and he only entered two. Now, the hardest stretch?

x061.text: Ahead lay the Moheyan Desert: over 800 li, no birds above, no beasts below, no water or grass.

x062.text: Ever wondered how one man and a horse could walk that far?

x063.text: But 100-odd li on, he got lost and missed Wild Horse Spring.

x064.text: He dismounted to drink; the bag was heavy, it slipped, and all of it spilled. The biography: his stake for a thousand li, gone at once.

x065.text: He turned east for 10-odd li, stopped, told himself: better to die going west than live by going back east.

x066.text: He turned his horse northwest again.

x067.text: This leg took four nights and five days. He drank not a drop, couldn't go on, and collapsed on the sand.

x068.text: The biography: those days, he silently called on Guanyin. This time, who'd save him?

x069.text: Midnight of day five: a sudden cool wind, cold as plunging into cold water.

x070.text: Remember the old red horse that knew the way? He got up; it stood too; they pressed on.

x071.text: Then he saw several acres of green grass, a clear pool beside it.

x072.text: Could one man make it out? He did. Two more days: out of the desert, into Yiwu.

x073.text: Gaochang's King Qu Wentai sent for him.

x074.text: The king wanted him as state teacher; he refused, fasting 3 days, not even water. Let him go?

x075.text: Day four, the king yielded; before the Buddha and his mother they swore brotherhood.

x076.text: So how did the novel turn his sworn brother into the emperor?

x077.text: Recall the opening's sworn brother and travel pass?

x078.text: The Ming novel Journey to the West: Taizong bows four times with him, sees him off himself.

x079.text: The novel's trip took 14 years; in the histories, he set off with no travel pass.

x080.text: The king gave him funds for 20 years, 24 letters of introduction, and wrote the Western Turkic khagan: the Master is my brother.

x081.text: Before leaving, he promised the king to stay three years in Gaochang on his way back. Did he keep it?

x082.text: No. Back in 640, Zhenguan 14, the Tang had already destroyed Gaochang.

x083.text: By the time he came back, that city was no longer a kingdom.

x084.text: At Khotan, homeward, he memorialized Taizong; it's in the Ci'en Biography.

x085.text: Eight characters in it are, we think, the most important in this file.

x086.text: "Defied statutes, went privately to India": he broke the law, went on his own.

x087.text: He owned up to sneaking abroad.

x088.text: In the same memorial he says he covered over 50,000 li, and, as customary: by the emperor's might, no obstacle anywhere.

x089.text: Sent to Chang'an, how would the emperor reply?

x090.text: 7 or 8 months on, the envoy returned. Taizong: I hear you sought the Way afar and are back; come see me soon.

x091.text: In the first month of 645, he reached Chang'an, 20 horses bearing 657 scriptures.

x092.text: But the emperor was away in Luoyang, readying war in Liaodong.

x093.text: 2nd month, Yiluan Hall, Luoyang Palace: he met Taizong. Recall the question? The emperor's first words:

x095.text: He replied: two or three memorials, none granted, so I went myself. Going abroad unbidden: the crime of presumption.

x096.text: Taizong: risking your life for the Dharma, to benefit all beings, I praise it. No need for shame.

x097.text: Recall the Yumen Pass debt? Ci'en Biography: in one line, the emperor wrote it off.

x098.text: Pardon aside, the Tang's own books clash on a number: what year did he cross the frontier?

x099.text: Remember 629? The Ci'en Biography, Continued Biographies, Records of the Western Regions all say it.

x100.text: Only a memorial attributed to him, in the Guang Hongming Ji, says Zhenguan 1: 627.

x102.text: The Old Book of Tang: just "early Zhenguan," no word of the warrant.

x103.text: Later scholars debated both years too. We think the side with more records holds up better, but won't rule.

x104.text: Back to the opening question: did he sneak abroad?

x105.text: So, this file: going abroad unbidden, on record; the year he set out, still open.

x106.text: As Guazhou's Li Chang, would you tear up the warrant? Tell me.

x107.text: This channel tells only what records hold. Subscribe to open files with us.
